items.title: The solopreneur shift reaches primary care as the portfolio clinician
items.body: The forces in this edition — AI filling the roles you once hired for — apply to medicine's small-business layer: locum GPs, small private clinics, single-handed practices. If NLW is right, an AI stack for letters, coding, bookkeeping and website makes small independent practice viable again after years of consolidation into super-partnerships; the economics that killed the single-hander partially reverse. If Zitron is right, that stack is priced below cost and a clinician who builds a lean practice around £50-a-month tools should budget for those tools tripling in price or vanishing — keep the practice viable without them.

items.title: Tesla's token cap is coming to the NHS in some form
items.body: Tesla capping engineers at 200 dollars a week of AI spend is the first famous example of usage-based rationing, and NHS procurement will not be far behind: once scribes and triage tools bill per consultation or per token rather than per seat, ICBs will set budgets and practices will be asked to justify usage. Worth quietly measuring now what the scribe actually saves per session — minutes per consultation, letters per clinic — so the case exists before the accountant asks for it.

items.title: The risk-calculus flip applies to medical careers too
items.body: NLW's sharpest point is that AI has scrambled which career path counts as safe. In medicine the analogue is the salaried-versus-portfolio question: if traditional employers become less necessary, the clinicians best placed are those with a tradeable skill plus AI leverage — the medical educator, the report-writing expert, the private specialist — rather than those betting everything on one employer's org chart. Advice worth passing to trainees choosing between a substantive post and a portfolio path.
